## A biomarker that changes its mind

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
In a late-stage oncology trial, one baseline biomarker looked **unassociated
with survival**.

A standard survival model scored its effect at ≈ 0.
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 7.0
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: "100%"
sign_flip_fig()
```
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center; font-size:1.0em; margin-top:-.3em;"}
**Harmful early. Protective late.** The two halves cancelled out.
:::

::: notes
OPEN HERE. Do not start with methods. Start with the curve crossing zero.
The point of the whole first act: averaging over time hid a real signal.
Pause after "the two halves cancelled out." That is the hook.

The y-axis says which way is worse. Say it once: "below zero is worse survival".
Survival statisticians read a negative Cox coefficient as protective, so do not
let the sign go unstated.

DISCLOSURE: no compound, gene, trial or variable name anywhere in this talk.
This figure is a redrawn schematic, captioned as illustrative - the study
figures could not be used because the labels are burned into the images.
If asked in Q&A: "the specific biomarker isn't something I can name here,
but the published analysis is in the reference on the last slide."
:::

## orthoMTL: don't average over time {background-color="#F5F5F5"}

::: columns
::: {.column width="42%"}
Cut follow-up into **landmarks**. Each one is a yes/no task: *still event-free?*

Fit all the tasks **at once** — sharing strength where they agree, each keeping
**its own effect**.
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| out-width: "100%"
landmark_fig()
```

::: {style="font-size:.5em; color:#939393; text-align:center; margin-top:-.2em;"}
Survival-as-multi-task framing after MTLSA (Li et al., KDD 2016).
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center; font-size:1.25em; margin-top:.3em;"}
**`github.com/Novartis/orthoMTL`** — on CRAN, 2026
:::

::: notes
This is the promotion slide. 35 seconds, no more. The sell is: if your outcome is
time-to-event and you suspect effects change over time, this package will show you that.
Built first for regression and classification; survival is the newest use.
Vervier 2014 (method), Juric 2026 Annals of Oncology (application).

EXPECT THIS QUESTION from biostatisticians: "isn't this just non-proportional hazards?
Why not coxph with tt(), a landmark Cox model, or RMST?" Do not fight it - those are
the right tools for a handful of covariates with an assumed shape of change.
[VERIFY BEFORE USE - draft answer] orthoMTL is aimed at many candidate features at
once: the landmark tasks are fitted jointly with a penalty, so effects can differ
between landmarks without a parametric time function, and tasks borrow strength
where the data say they agree.
:::

## PhD code to CRAN: the first catch was a test

::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
Twelve-year-old research code, packaged by an **AI agent**: a language model
that edits files and runs commands itself.

::: {.fragment fragment-index="1"}
Writing tests for the **logistic loss**, it found a **real bug** in my 2014
gradient: labels were ±1, the code used the 0/1 formula. I confirmed it by hand.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index="2" style="margin-top:.4em;"}
The test: flip every label and the probabilities **must** mirror. They didn't.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index="2"}
```r
fit_a <- fit(X,  y)
fit_b <- fit(X, -y)  # flipped
expect_equal(predict(fit_a, X),
             1 - predict(fit_b, X))
```

::: {style="font-size:.5em; color:#939393;"}
Sketch of the idea, not the package's actual test.
:::
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
Keep this tight. The transferable idea is the symmetry check, not the bug: a check a
machine can run caught what twelve years of reading the code did not. That is the
first piece of evidence for the take-home.
Facts to state exactly: the agent found the bug while writing unit tests for the
logistic loss; I verified by hand that it was a real error; the code was then
modified. Do not claim I designed the test, and do not claim the agent
"understood" the maths - say it found it and I confirmed it.
:::

## Then CRAN rejected us. Twice. {background-color="#F5F5F5"}

::: {style="font-size:1.5em; line-height:1.9; margin-top:.5em;"}
::: {.fragment}
**1.** An invalid `LICENSE` field.
:::
::: {.fragment}
**2.** A hard-coded `set.seed()`.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:1.15em; margin-top:.7em; color:#FF4E00;"}
Neither was caught by any automated check. Both were caught by **a CRAN volunteer**.
:::

::: notes
Big type, slow delivery. This is the pivot from act one to act two.
Both rejections cost round-trips measured in weeks of calendar time.
CRAN is maintained by volunteers - the Repository Policy says so in its own
preamble: "CRAN is maintained by the efforts of volunteers (the CRAN team)".
Their time is described there as CRAN's most precious resource. That matters for
the argument: the scarce reviewing capacity is human and unpaid.
:::

## What is a skill file?

::: columns
::: {.column width="42%"}
A **Markdown file of instructions**, loaded into the agent's context before it
starts work.

Posit and others publish CRAN ones. People drop them into their projects.

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.6em; font-weight:700;"}
Would one have got us through CRAN in one shot?
:::
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
```markdown
# CRAN submission notes for this package

This package was submitted to CRAN before and
rejected twice by human reviewers. Passing the
check is necessary but is not enough.

## 1. Do not set a seed to a specific number
##    inside a function
- Search every file in `R/` for `set.seed(`.
- Give the function a `seed = NULL` argument ...
```

::: {style="font-size:.5em; color:#939393;"}
Excerpt (abridged): the file I later wrote from our own two rejections — last backup slide.
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
Thirty seconds. Many people in the room have never seen one; the point is that it is
just text, there is no magic. In this study the file was always loaded (as CLAUDE.md),
not fetched on demand.

The question is the counterfactual: the package is already on CRAN, after two rounds
of human review on things R CMD check never printed. Would a skill file have saved them?
:::

## We ran it like a trial

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| out-width: "100%"
design_fig()
```

::: notes
Lean into the trial vocabulary - this room owns it: arms, control, blinding,
pre-registration. Say "we ran it like a five-arm trial". Walk the diagram left to right
in one breath each: the starting package (four planted defects, plus our original
hard-coded set.seed); block-randomised into five arms, every arm once per block in
random order; scored blind. Then the one point that matters for later: we expected the
machine check to floor, so the protocol made the AI judge the primary measure.

The control has n=20 because a second batch of 10 runs was meant to carry a hindsight
file and never received it - a protocol deviation, told on the "not claiming" slide.
Those runs are identical in configuration to the control, so they are pooled.

Skills from posit-dev/skills (checklist = cran-extrachecks, general R =
r-package-development) and CoryMcCartan/agent-skills (process = cran-submit); the
handbook arm had the raw CRAN docs loaded into context. Backup has the table.

IMPORTANT framing. Do NOT say "nobody measures skill files" - that is false and
someone in this room will know it. Skills ARE measured; the useful point is that
the measurements are already conditional, and I am adding one more condition.
The literature was already hedging: skills "often provide no benefit, and can even
hurt" (SkillDelta, Xu et al. 2026; SkillAxe, Gautam et al. 2026).

SAY THIS OUT LOUD, one sentence, no defensiveness:
"The biggest study, SkillsBench, does find a solid average gain - but on 87
tasks hand-picked to be easier with a skill, and not one of them is R."
If it comes up in Q&A: its tasks are admitted only when "significantly easier
with Skills", its skills are top-quartile quality, and its software-engineering
domain gains the second-least of eight (+11.6 pp). Backup slide has the detail.
:::

## Every arm hit the ceiling {background-color="#161616" style="color:#FCFCFC"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:.1em;"}
::: {style="font-size:5em; font-weight:700; color:#FF4E00; line-height:1;"}
`r n_seed`/`r n_runs`
:::
::: {style="font-size:1.3em; margin-top:.2em;"}
runs fixed all four planted defects — **control included**
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center; font-size:1.0em; margin-top:.7em;"}
No skill file beat no skill file. A **ceiling**, not a null: three of the four
are defects `R CMD check` reports.
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center; font-size:1.0em; margin-top:.6em; color:#FF4E00; font-weight:700;"}
So a skill file could only help where the check is silent.
:::

::: notes
THE PUNCH. Stop talking for two seconds after the number appears.
Then: "including the control, all twenty runs of it."

Say "ceiling" before anyone in the room does. The machine-checked result is a
secondary endpoint and it floored, exactly as the pre-registration predicted.

The LICENSE defect that actually got us rejected - the one planted defect R CMD check
does not report - was fixed in every run, in every arm, control included.

The last fragment is the hinge into the next two slides. Do not skip it.
:::

## Why the control did so well

::: {style="font-size:1.2em; margin-top:.6em;"}
::: {.fragment}
The agent runs **`R CMD check`** and reads its own failures.
:::
::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.6em;"}
A machine check beats a checklist: it reflects **this** package, **today**.
:::
::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.6em; color:#FF4E00; font-weight:700;"}
Skill files add little where a tool already tells the truth.
:::
:::

::: notes
This is the mechanistic explanation and the most useful thing in the deck.
Not an argument against skill files - an argument about where they pay. The CRAN
rules a skill encodes are mostly the ones R CMD check already enforces.

Not unique to us (say only if asked): SkillFlow found agents used retrieved skills
70% of the time and still gained nothing. Reading a skill is not the same as needing one.

If asked "but models keep improving, so isn't the checklist point moot?" - that
cuts in my favour, not against. A better model needs the checklist less, not
more. My claim is about the tool being authoritative for this package today,
not about the checklist being stale in the abstract.

If asked "then why do people write CRAN skill files?" - three honest reasons.
(1) Most were written against weaker models, where the gap was real.
(2) They encode the part R CMD check cannot see - which is the next slide.
(3) Writing one is cheap and feels responsible; nobody had measured whether it
works on this job, which is why I ran this.
:::

## Where the check is silent: `set.seed()` {.smaller}

The starting package called `set.seed(42)` inside four exported functions — our
second rejection. `R CMD check` says nothing.

| Arm | n | Canonical fix (`seed = NULL`) | Default kept, RNG restored | Still hard-coded |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Control | 20 | **0** | 10 | 10 |
| Checklist | 9 | 0 | 8 | 1 |
| Process | 9 | **7** | 1 | 1 |
| General R | 10 | 0 | 7 | 3 |
| Handbook | 9 | **8** | 0 | 1 |

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.4em;"}
Afterwards, a file quoting the reviewer: **10/10** canonical fixes, against **0/10**
for a fresh control.
:::

::: {style="margin-top:.4em; color:#939393;"}
Exploratory: re-scored after unblinding, n = 9–20, no test. A lead, not a result.
:::

::: notes
This is where instructions seem to matter: the one real rejection the tool cannot see.
The control produced the canonical fix zero times in twenty runs; the process skill and
the raw handbook mostly did. Every arm had the Cookbook text on disk, so "on disk" was
not enough; why text in context helps, I can't say.

Say the caveats in the same breath, in this order: (1) my original detector only matched
set.seed(<literal>) and scored zero hits on the starting package itself, so I fixed the
rule after unblinding; (2) the re-score is a pure function of the package files with no
access to arm labels, so the timing cannot have biased the direction; (3) counts are
descriptive, n = 9-20, no test.

"Default kept" means seed = 42 stays but goes through a helper that restores the user's
RNG state - arguably acceptable, not what the reviewer asked for.

The 10/10 line is an after-the-fact positive control: different CLI version, labels
known, no judge, and the file contains the answer. It shows the defect is learnable
from text in context - nothing more. Backup slides have both.
:::

## The AI judge measured itself {background-color="#161616" style="color:#FCFCFC"}

::: {style="font-size:1.1em; margin-top:.3em;"}
The judge was the primary measure — it was meant to see what the tool cannot.
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.6em;"}
It had **12 criteria**. Ten never fired.
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.6em;"}
One that did: our maintainer email — **unchanged in all 57 runs**.<br>
The judge called it fine in **10**, a problem in **47**.
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.6em;"}
Same text, opposite verdicts. The only other criterion that fired did the same.
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.7em; color:#FF4E00; font-weight:700; text-align:center; font-size:1.1em;"}
Every "finding" was my instrument. Not my arms.
:::

::: notes
This is the real result and I should say so plainly.

I did not find this during scoring. I found it afterwards, reading the judge's
own evidence strings - which I did not have to look at. That is the point worth
making to this audience: the failure was invisible at the summary level. The
counts looked like a clean two-criterion signal. Only the free-text justification
showed the judge arguing both sides of the same fact.

The other criterion, if asked: one sentence in the starting package - flagged in 23
trees, excused in 2, and in 29 the judge never opened the file (3 n/a).

If asked "so is the whole experiment void?" - no. The machine-check result stands
on its own; it came from R CMD check, not the judge. What is void is the idea that
the judge added sensitivity on top of it - and the judge was the pre-registered
primary conformance measure, so on what a human reviewer would object to, I have
no working endpoint.

Do not oversell this as a general claim about LLM judges. It is one package, one
rubric, one rep per tree.

The email story (judge right for the wrong reason; we are changing it in 0.2.0 anyway)
is in backup. Only tell it if there is time in Q&A.
:::

## What I am *not* claiming {.smaller}

- **Not** "skill files are useless" → where tasks are *selected* to need them, they help;
  this is *no benefit on the machine-checkable part of CRAN prep, with the docs at hand*
- **N = 1** on every axis that matters: one package, one agent model (Claude Opus 5.5 in
  Claude Code), and a judge from the **same vendor**. Runs were not powered
- **A protocol deviation**: one planned treatment arm got placebo — its file never reached
  the model. Caught afterwards by the size of the first prompt (a drug-level check); those
  10 runs joined the control
- **No working measure of what humans object to**: the judge had no sensitivity, and the
  `set.seed()` contrast is a post-hoc lead

::: notes
Say these out loud and quickly. Credibility is the currency of a null result.
Lead with the non-claim, then the reason.

The protocol deviation, told as a pharma audience will hear it: the arm meant to carry a
hindsight file written from our own rejections ran ten times with no file at all. Its
first API call was 7,145 tokens in every run - identical to the control - while every
real skill arm was larger. The freeze checklist had no box for "the file exists". The
pooling decision was made on that instrument evidence, not on outcomes. See
LESSONS_LEARNED.md section 0.

The lost runs go here, orally: 3 runs died on API rate limits - infrastructure, not
agent behaviour - so `r n_runs` of 60 are analysed. Excluded, not rerun: a replayed run
weeks later under different rate limits is not the same experimental unit, and rerunning
after unblinding would have been the only part of this experiment scored with the labels
known. Two of the three died at 1 turn having spent $0.00.

Sample size, if asked: n=5 per arm was never powered. After an interim unblinded look at
n=5 we extended to 10 per arm because time and budget allowed, not to chase a result;
counts are descriptive. Do not claim a pre-registered n=10.

Ceiling: 3 of 4 planted defects are visible to R CMD check, and every arm had the
Cookbook on disk.

If I am running long this compresses to one sentence: "three runs died on rate
limits, 57 analysed, excluded not rerun." See LESSONS_LEARNED.md §11.
:::

## Take home {background-color="#F5F5F5"}

::: {style="font-size:1.05em; line-height:1.45;"}
::: {.fragment}
**1.** Effects that change over time hide in averages. Fit the landmarks
**jointly** → `orthoMTL`
:::
::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.35em;"}
**2.** Agents are good at what a **machine** can check. Invest in **executable
checks** first — tests, `R CMD check` — and spend prose on what no tool sees.
:::
::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.35em;"}
**3.** My primary instrument, an AI judge, measured itself. Check a judge
**against itself** before you trust it.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.5em; text-align:center; font-size:1.2em; color:#FF4E00; font-weight:700;"}
Machine checks are cheap. Judgement isn't.
:::

::: notes
The three points escalate: the science, the practical advice, the thing that cost me
a month to learn. Point 2 carries all three pieces of evidence: the label-flip test,
R CMD check flooring every arm, and set.seed as the place where prose seemed to matter.

Land the closing line slowly. It is the thesis of the whole talk, not a sign-off -
the experiment is the evidence for it. Earlier wording, if preferred: "Generation got
cheap. Verification did not." The new one says what the data show: verification by
a machine was cheap and worked; verification by judgement was the expensive part.
:::

::: {style="font-size:.55em; margin-top:.3em; text-align:center;"}
[`github.com/Novartis/orthoMTL`](https://github.com/Novartis/orthoMTL) · Vervier et al. 2014 · Juric et al. 2026 · full references in backup
:::

Snapshot captured **2026-09-18**, identical across all 60 runs.

The handbook arm loaded this text directly into context; the other arms were told where it was.

::: notes
This is the HANDBOOK/COMMUNITY provenance boundary: a criterion derivable from
these three documents is HANDBOOK, anything else is COMMUNITY.
If asked why the control is not "no information at all" — because that is not the
realistic alternative. The real alternative is a competent person with the docs.
:::

## Backup: the hedges, in their own words {.smaller}

| Finding | Source |
|:--|:--|
| Skills "often provide no benefit, and can even hurt performance while incurring additional token costs" | SkillDelta, Xu et al. 2026 |
| Human-authored skills +16.2 pp; **LLM-authored skills give no measurable gain** | SkillAxe, Gautam et al. 2026 |
| Agents used retrieved skills 70% of the time yet showed **no performance gain** where the corpus lacked good skills for the domain | SkillFlow, Li et al. 2026 |
| Self-generated skills landed **below** the no-skills baseline (−8 to −11.5 pp) | SkillsBench, Li et al. 2026 |

My null is the same shape, in a domain none of them covered.

## Backup: the counterweight {.smaller}

The headline positive result is **SkillsBench**: curated skills lift pass rate
33.9% → 50.5% (**+16.6 pp**) across 87 tasks and 18 model–harness configurations.
I am not disputing it. Three things make it a different question from mine:

- **8 domains** — natural science, media, cybersecurity, industrial, finance, office, software engineering, maths/OR. **No R, no packaging, no CRAN**
- Tasks are admitted only if **"significantly easier with Skills"**; no-separation tasks are rejected as low-signal
- Skills are drawn from the **top quality quartile** (10.1/12 vs ecosystem mean 6.2/12); the authors call this "an optimistic scenario"

Their own domain gradient points my way: **software engineering +11.6 pp**,
second-lowest of eight, against natural science **+28.8 pp** — "domains with
stronger pretraining and tooling coverage benefit less."

::: notes
Use this slide only if challenged. The honest summary: SkillsBench asks "how much
can a good skill help where a skill should help?" I ask "did a skill help on the
job I actually had?" My four defects were not chosen for skill-dependence, and
three of four are machine-detectable. The two results bracket the same effect
from opposite ends rather than conflicting.
:::

## Backup: the three ways we checked correctness {.smaller}

| Check | What it proves |
|:--|:--|
| Against the old validated package | identical coefficients on 5 fixed cases |
| Flip every label | answer must flip; `0.62` → `0.000` |
| Simulated data, known truth | recovers the right features, 10/10 seeds |

::: notes
The survival path is exactly where comparing against the old code cannot reach —
there was no old survival code. That is why the simulation oracle exists.
:::

## Backup: our own maintainer address {.smaller}

Even a noisy judge can be right once. It flagged our own maintainer address in
47 of 57 trees: `kevin.vervier@novartis.com`

CRAN requires **a person, not a mailing list**, kept current and reachable
"**without any form of filtering**". A corporate account is one re-org away
from failing all three. **Not a violation today. Changing in 0.2.0 anyway.**

::: notes
Tell only if there is time in Q&A, and tell it precisely or someone will correct me.

It is NOT currently against the rules - a named person at a company address is
compliant. The exposure is filtering and job changes, both anticipated by the
policy language. Say "not a violation today" out loud; do not oversell it.

Do NOT say "a newer model spotted this". It is criterion C13, it was in the
corpus from the start. A broken instrument can still be right once; that is not
evidence it works.

No arm ever changed the address - it is still the same in all 57 runs. The 10
COMPLIANT verdicts (7 of them in the handbook arm) are the judge excusing the
corporate domain because Novartis Pharma AG is also the listed copyright holder.
That is judge variance on an under-specified criterion, not an arm fixing anything.
:::

## Backup: what I would change {.smaller}

- Score **R01 (`set.seed()`)** with a rule that also sees seeds passed as default arguments
- Plant more defects only a **CRAN volunteer** could catch, and calibrate the judge on them
- A **positive control** in the blinded run, plus a pre-flight check that each arm's file reaches the model
- A **handicapped arm** with the CRAN docs removed: if it does worse, the measurement has teeth
- Judge each package several times, not once
- More packages, more models

## Backup: the four planted defects {.smaller}

| Defect | Caught by `R CMD check`? | Repaired |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `NAMESPACE` deleted | yes — check cannot even run | 57/57 |
| `usethis` LICENSE template vs GPL-3 DESCRIPTION | **no** — this is rejection **R02** | **57/57** |
| DESCRIPTION metadata (`Authors@R`, title case) | yes | 57/57 |
| Unused declared `Imports` | yes | 57/57 |

Three of four are machine-visible. Our other real rejection — **R01, the
hard-coded `set.seed()`** — was left in the starting package as a fifth defect that
`R CMD check` does not report; it is on the next slide.

Three of four machine-visible is the result's main caveat: this measures the
easy half of CRAN preparation.

## Backup: the hard-coded seed (R01) {.smaller}

The starting package defaulted `seed = 42` and called `set.seed()` unconditionally in
four exported functions — the exact pattern CRAN rejected. `R CMD check` does not report it.

Counts per arm are on the `set.seed()` slide. Completed runs only; descriptive counts, no test. "Default
kept" means `seed = 42` stays but the value goes through a helper that restores the user's RNG
state — arguably acceptable, not what the reviewer asked for. The control includes the 10 runs
that were meant to carry the hindsight file and did not (see arms slide).

**These counts are a re-score, run after unblinding.** My original rule only matched
`set.seed(<literal>)` inside a function body, so it scored **zero hits on the starting package itself** — a
detector that cannot see the defect it was built for. I found that while preparing this talk, fixed
the rule, and re-ran it. The re-score reads package files only and never touches the blind map: the
same code at first unblinding would have produced this same table. The flaw was in the detector, not
in the direction of the correction.

::: notes
Be upfront - I planted what I could verify automatically, which is exactly the
half where the control was always going to do well. The honest version of this
experiment seeds the other half, and that is the first thing I would change.

On the post-unblinding point, say it before anyone asks, and say it in this order:
(1) the rule was wrong, (2) here is how it was wrong, (3) it is a pure function of
tree content, so the timing cannot have biased the direction. rescore_r01.R takes
a tree path and returns hits; it has no access to arm labels. Validated on 8
synthetic cases, the starting package (3 hits), baseline and control (0), and a mutant (1).

I am NOT claiming this as a skill-file win. Two things block that. It is one
criterion at n=9-10 with no test, and it is a post-hoc re-score. The controls
(n=20, including the 10 runs that never got the hindsight file) produced the canonical fix zero times in 20 runs, which
makes the process/handbook contrast more interesting, not proven. Report it as the most
interesting loose end in the dataset and move on.

If asked why the process and handbook arms and nobody else: the cookbook contains the canonical
seed = NULL pattern verbatim, in a section every arm could read. The handbook arm had that text
front-loaded into context rather than pointed at; the process skill is the adversarial-review
arm. That is a hypothesis about front-loading vs distillation, not a finding.
:::

## Backup: positive control, run afterwards (R01) {.smaller}

The hindsight file was written from CRAN's own two rejection messages, installed, and checked to
reach the model (first-call context +1,055 tokens over its paired control). Then a fresh control and the
hindsight arm were run as 10 interleaved pairs, **after unblinding, labels known**, on a newer
Claude Code (2.1.294).

| Arm | n | Canonical fix (`seed = NULL`) | Default kept | Still hard-coded |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Fresh control | 10 | 0 | 6 | 4 |
| Hindsight file delivered | 10 | 10 | 0 | 0 |

Two extra hindsight runs without a surviving partner (rate limits) were also canonical: 12 of 12.
This is a ceiling check, not a skill-file result: the file contains the answer. It shows the
seed defect is learnable from text in context, which the blinded experiment could not show. Not
pooled with the 57; no judge panel was run on these trees. `R CMD check` was identical across
arms: no errors or warnings in any of the 22 trees. Scripts and scores: `supplementary/`.

::: notes
Frame as an afterward positive control. Do NOT say the blinded experiment would have given the
same result: different CLI version, labels known, no judge. The claim is only that when the file
is delivered, the instrument sees the fix.
:::
